results.fact: Season this route is actually climbed in
results.evidence: Research supports the season field more than the reader assumed: SummitPost says there is no trail, the peak is often a moderate-to-difficult bushwhack in spring and summer, and it is therefore rarely done in summer; WTA and The Mountaineers present Tye Peak as an extension of the Skyline Lake snowshoe/ski trip; the one detailed ascent found (stevensong) is a winter one. Summer ascents exist but are rare, so neither a flat 'Nov-Apr' nor the summer-only framing of best_season/seasonal_guidance is clearly right; settling it means choosing which outing this row describes. The season field also carries explanation text that belongs in best_season.

WTA gives 1,100-1,300 ft to Skyline Lake/the ridge and says the Tye Peak extension more than doubles the total gain (>2,200-2,600 ft), which favours gain_ft ~2,400 over 1,800; Mountaineers activity listings give inconsistent figures (1,500 ft; 3,300 ft on a ski tour). Row geometry (4,061 -> 5,200 gap -> 4,800 creek -> 5,476, regaining the gap on the way out) gives ~2,200 ft car-to-car, so the itinerary's 1,800 looks like the one-way ascent only. No two sources agree on a number, so nothing is patched.

results.fact: total elevation gain to the crag
results.evidence: Every source agrees 4,400 ft is too low: the trailhead sits near 1,200-1,300 ft and Lake Viviane near 6,785 ft (net ~5,500). A Snow Lakes trail guide says Lake Viviane is reached at 9.3 mi 'after climbing 6,400 vertical feet'; the Forest Service gives 6,500 ft for the whole 12-mile trail to Perfection Lake (further and higher than Viviane). The cumulative figure to Viviane therefore lies somewhere between ~5,500 and 6,400 and no two sources agree on it, so gain_ft and the waypoint note are left for follow-up (gain_ft is clearly understated).

results.fact: How long consolidated/climbable snow lasts on the route
results.evidence: The one detailed first-hand account found (trailcatjim, June 1-3 2020) met rock-hard snow and the 70-degree snowfinger, but describes that snowpack as exceptionally large for the date and says it blocked the normal summer scramble; a later WTA report found only thin snow cover and low Class 4 rock at the summit block. That suggests the route is normally a summer rock scramble with snow as an early-season condition, which disagrees with parts of both season and best_season; no two sources give a snow window, so nothing is patched.

results.fact: route grade — 4th class vs a roped 5.6 pitch
results.evidence: Sources disagree on what this face is: the East Face route page gives 4th class (zig-zagging ledges on the E/SE side, a short 4th-class hand crack, 'sturdy boots' as the protection, reverse the route to descend), while SummitPost describes a Southeast Face line up the white rock in one pitch of 5.6. The row blends both (4th-class grade and pitch_detail vs the '5.6 pitch' in the itinerary and descent_text, and white-rock wording in the base finding). Choosing which line this row describes needs a decision; no patch.

The East Face route page says to reverse the route to descend (agreeing with `descent` and `bail`); descent_text and the approach variant say most parties go down the South Face/Southwest Corner side instead. Only one source was found, and it backs the shorter field, which is hidden behind the longer descent_text on screen; not settled by two sources.

results.fact: crux grade — rock_grade omits it, and 5.4 vs 5.5 elsewhere
results.evidence: The 5.5 step-up (sharp ridge 100 ft above the col, traverse right onto the South Face at Class 4, 5.5 step, 4-ft summit slot) is The Mountaineers' description of the Southwest Corner route. Their South Face route is listed as an alpine scramble: head toward the white wall, traverse an exposed slabby ledge around to the east side and scramble large black blocks to the summit; Wikipedia rates the tower class 3. No source gives 5.4. The row's beta follows the scramble while grade/pitch_detail (5.4, 2 pitches) and three 5.5 mentions follow the roped corner, so the fix is a restructure of the route (grade, pitches, rack, partner requirements), not a number swap.
